Customer Dataset Overview¶

We begin EDA by inspecting the customer dataset:

  • Size: 1,000 customers, 9 attributes
  • Data quality: No missing values, correct data types
  • Key variables:
    • Age: 18–75 (mean ~46), balanced distribution across quartiles
    • NumChildren: 0–4 (mean ~1.3), majority have 0–2 children
    • JoinDate: July 2020 – July 2024, median July 2022 → steady acquisition trend

Insights:

  • The customer base is largely middle-aged (30–60 years).
  • Family size is small, which may affect purchasing behavior.
  • Acquisition has been consistent over 4 years, with half of customers joining after mid-2022.

_Univariate analysis (single variable)¶

In [16]:
plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
sns.histplot(df_customers['Age'], bins=20, kde=True, color='royalblue', edgecolor='black')

plt.title("Customer Age Distribution", fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', color='darkblue')
plt.xlabel("Age", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.ylabel("Number of Customers", fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')

plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)

plt.show()

Age Distribution Analysis¶

As part of the exploratory data analysis (EDA), we examine the distribution of customer ages.
The histogram above shows the frequency of customers across different age ranges, with a kernel density estimate (KDE) overlay to highlight the overall trend.

Insights:

  • Most customers fall between ages 25 and 45, indicating a younger demographic base.
  • There is a gradual decline in customer count beyond age 50, suggesting fewer older customers in the dataset.
  • The KDE curve provides a smooth estimate of the probability density, confirming that the distribution is slightly right-skewed.

Business Relevance:

  • Promotions can be targeted toward the dominant age group (25–45).
  • Specialized campaigns may be designed for older customers to improve engagement in that segment.

_Bivariate analysis (two variables)¶

In [17]:
plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
sns.countplot(x='Gender', data=df_customers, palette='Set2')
plt.title("Customer Count by Gender", fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.xlabel("Gender")
plt.ylabel("Number of Customers")
plt.show()

Bivariate Analysis: Customer Count by Gender¶

The countplot above compares the number of customers across gender categories.

Insights:

  • The distribution is relatively balanced among Male, Female, and Not Disclosed groups, each contributing close to one-third of the customer base.
  • This balance suggests that the dataset is diverse and not heavily skewed toward one gender.
  • The presence of a significant "Not Disclosed" group highlights that some customers prefer not to reveal gender information, which is important for respecting privacy in segmentation.

Business Relevance:

  • Balanced gender representation means marketing strategies should remain inclusive rather than overly targeted to one group.
  • Campaigns can be designed to appeal broadly, while still offering tailored promotions for specific demographics.
  • The "Not Disclosed" segment should be considered in analysis, as these customers may respond better to neutral, non-gendered campaigns.

_Categorical variable analysis¶

In [18]:

Categorical Variable Analysis: Customer Count by City¶

The bar chart above shows the distribution of customers across major Indian cities.

Insights:

  • Jaipur has the highest customer count, slightly above 110, indicating strong market presence in that region.
  • Kolkata and Chennai have the lowest counts, around 90, suggesting smaller customer bases compared to other cities.
  • Other cities such as Delhi, Pune, Hyderabad, and Mumbai show moderate representation, each contributing significantly to the overall dataset.

Business Relevance:

  • Cities with larger customer bases (e.g., Jaipur, Delhi) may warrant more aggressive marketing campaigns and inventory allocation.
  • Underrepresented cities (e.g., Kolkata, Chennai) could be targeted with localized promotions to boost engagement and growth.
  • Comparing city distribution with other attributes (e.g., age, gender, spending behavior) can uncover regional differences in customer demographics and preferences.

_Correlation heatmap (multivariate)¶

In [19]:
plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))
sns.heatmap(df_customers.select_dtypes(include='number').corr(), 
            annot=True, cmap='coolwarm')
plt.title("Correlation Heatmap (Numeric Features)")
plt.show()

Correlation Heatmap (Numeric Features)¶

The heatmap above shows the correlation between numeric variables in the customer dataset — specifically Age and NumChildren.

Insights:

  • Each variable is perfectly correlated with itself (correlation = 1).
  • The correlation between Age and NumChildren is -0.04, indicating a very weak negative relationship.
  • This suggests that as age increases, the number of children tends to decrease slightly, but the relationship is not strong enough to be statistically meaningful.

Business Relevance:

  • Since the correlation is weak, age and family size should be treated as largely independent factors in customer segmentation.
  • Marketing strategies should consider both attributes separately — for example:
    • Age groups for lifestyle or fashion targeting.
    • Family size for household or family-oriented product promotions.
  • Combining these variables in multivariate analysis (e.g., clustering or RFM segmentation) may reveal deeper patterns not captured by simple correlation.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) – Transactions Dataset¶

We begin by examining the structure and summary statistics of the transactions data.

Dataset Overview¶

  • Size: 23,050 transaction records
  • Columns:
    • CustomerID – unique identifier for each customer
    • TransactionDate – date of transaction (2020–2025)
    • TransactionAmount – monetary value of each transaction
  • Data Quality: No missing values, correct data types (object, datetime64, float64)

Descriptive Statistics¶

  • Transaction Amounts:

    • Mean: ~1000
    • Range: 3.87 – 6890
    • Standard deviation: ~703 → indicates variability in spending
    • Distribution: Right-skewed, with most transactions clustered around 500–1300 and a few high-value outliers

  • Transaction Dates:

    • Range: August 2020 – July 2025
    • Median: April 2024 → half of transactions occurred after this date
    • Quartiles show steady activity across years, suggesting consistent customer engagement

Insights¶

  • Customers typically spend modest amounts, but a small group makes very high-value purchases.
  • Transaction activity has been consistent over 5 years, with no gaps in data.
  • The dataset is clean and ready for deeper analysis (RFM segmentation, trend analysis, customer profiling).

Business Relevance¶

  • Identifying high-value transactions helps target premium customers for loyalty programs.
  • Time-based analysis can reveal seasonal trends and guide promotional campaigns.
  • Clean, complete data ensures reliable segmentation and predictive modeling.

_Transaction amount distribution¶

Transaction Amount Distribution¶

The histogram above shows how transaction amounts are distributed across the dataset.

Insights:

  • The distribution is right-skewed: most transactions are below 1,000, while a few extend up to ~7,000.
  • A large cluster of transactions falls between 500–1,300, indicating typical spending behavior.
  • High-value outliers exist, but they are rare compared to the bulk of transactions.

Business Relevance:

  • Most customers make modest purchases, so promotions should target this spending range.
  • High-value transactions, though rare, represent premium customers who may benefit from loyalty programs or personalized offers.
  • Understanding this distribution helps in designing pricing strategies, detecting anomalies, and segmenting customers by spending behavior.

_Transactions over time¶

In [22]:
df_transactions['Month'] = df_transactions['TransactionDate'].dt.to_period('M')
monthly_sales = df_transactions.groupby('Month')['TransactionAmount'].sum()
monthly_sales.plot(kind='bar', figsize=(10,4))
plt.title("Monthly Sales Trend")
plt.ylabel("Total Transaction Amount")
plt.show()

Monthly Sales Trend Analysis¶

The bar chart above shows the total transaction amounts aggregated by month over the period August 2020 – July 2025.

Insights¶

  • Overall Growth: There is a clear upward trend in monthly sales, reflecting consistent business growth over the 5-year period.
  • Seasonality: Fluctuations are visible around 2024–2025, suggesting possible seasonal effects or promotional campaigns driving spikes in sales.
  • Stability: From 2020 through 2023, growth appears steady and gradual, indicating a stable customer base and reliable transaction flow.
  • Acceleration: The higher peaks in later years highlight increased customer engagement and potentially larger transaction values.

Business Relevance¶

  • Forecasting: The upward trend supports positive revenue projections and helps in planning future inventory and staffing.
  • Campaign Planning: Seasonal spikes can be leveraged to design targeted promotions during high-demand months.
  • Customer Engagement: Sustained growth suggests successful acquisition and retention strategies, which can be further optimized by focusing on peak months.

_Outlier detection¶

In [23]:
sns.boxplot(x=df_transactions['TransactionAmount'])
plt.title("Outlier Detection in Transaction Amounts")
plt.show()

Outlier Detection – Transaction Amounts¶

The box plot above highlights the distribution of transaction amounts and identifies potential outliers.

Insights¶

  • The central box (interquartile range) shows that most transactions fall between ~500 and 1,500.
  • The whiskers extend to ~3,000, capturing the bulk of typical transaction values.
  • Several points beyond the whiskers represent outliers, with amounts reaching up to ~7,000.
  • These outliers indicate customers who make unusually high-value purchases compared to the majority.

Business Relevance¶

  • Premium Customers: Outliers may represent high-value customers who contribute disproportionately to revenue. They are prime candidates for loyalty programs or personalized offers.
  • Risk Monitoring: Very large transactions could also signal anomalies or potential fraud, requiring closer monitoring.
  • Segmentation Strategy: Differentiating between typical spenders and outliers helps refine customer segmentation and marketing campaigns.

5. Perform RFM Calculation¶

In [25]:
# Reference date = max transaction date + 1
ref_date = df_transactions['TransactionDate'].max() + pd.Timedelta(days=1)

df_rfm = df_transactions.groupby('CustomerID').agg(
    Recency=('TransactionDate', lambda x: (ref_date - x.max()).days),
    Frequency=('TransactionDate', 'count'),
    Monetary=('TransactionAmount', 'sum')
)

6. Score RFM¶

In [27]:
# Quantile-based scoring
df_rfm['R_Score'] = pd.qcut(df_rfm['Recency'], 5, labels=[5,4,3,2,1]).astype(int)
df_rfm['F_Score'] = pd.qcut(df_rfm['Frequency'], 5, labels=[1,2,3,4,5]).astype(int)
df_rfm['M_Score'] = pd.qcut(df_rfm['Monetary'], 5, labels=[1,2,3,4,5]).astype(int)

# Combined RFM
df_rfm['RFM_Segment'] = df_rfm['R_Score'].astype(str) + df_rfm['F_Score'].astype(str) + df_rfm['M_Score'].astype(str)
df_rfm['RFM_Score'] = df_rfm[['R_Score','F_Score','M_Score']].sum(axis=1)

6. Assign Segment Labels¶

In [30]:
def segment(row):
    if row['RFM_Segment'] == '555':
        return 'Champion'
    elif row['R_Score'] >= 4 and row['F_Score'] >= 4:
        return 'Loyal Customer'
    elif row['R_Score'] >= 4 and row['F_Score'] <= 3:
        return 'Potential Loyalist'
    elif row['R_Score'] <= 2 and row['F_Score'] >= 3:
        return 'At Risk'
    elif row['R_Score'] == 1 and row['F_Score'] <= 2:
        return 'Lost'
    elif row['M_Score'] >= 4:
        return 'Big Spender'
    else:
        return 'Others'

df_rfm['Segment'] = df_rfm.apply(segment, axis=1)

plt.xlabel("Segment", fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel("Number of Customers", fontsize=12)
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Customer Segments Distribution Analysis¶

The bar chart illustrates the distribution of customers across different RFM-based segments. Key observations:

  • Potential Loyalists (252 customers) form the largest group, indicating many customers show promising buying behavior but need nurturing to become fully loyal.
  • At Risk (207 customers) is the second largest segment, highlighting a significant portion of customers who have reduced engagement and may churn if not reactivated.
  • Others (181 customers) represent a mixed group with moderate activity, requiring further profiling to design targeted strategies.
  • Loyal Customers (122 customers) demonstrate consistent purchasing patterns and should be rewarded to maintain retention.
  • Lost (105 customers) are inactive customers who may need win-back campaigns or can be deprioritized depending on business goals.
  • Big Spenders (98 customers) contribute high monetary value despite lower frequency, making them important for premium offers.
  • Champions (35 customers) are the most valuable segment, combining high recency, frequency, and monetary scores. They should be prioritized for loyalty programs and advocacy initiatives.

Insight:
The distribution shows that while the business has a strong base of Potential Loyalists, the high count of At Risk customers signals a need for proactive engagement strategies. Focusing on converting Potential Loyalists into Loyal Customers and retaining Champions will maximize long-term revenue and customer lifetime value.

Customer Segmentation Distribution (Donut Chart Analysis)¶

In [34]:
# Data
segments = [
    'Potential Loyalist', 'At Risk', 'Others',
    'Loyal Customer', 'Lost', 'Big Spender', 'Champion'
]
counts = [252, 207, 181, 122, 105, 98, 35]

# Colors for each segment
colors = [
    '#1f77b4', '#ff7f0e', '#7f7f7f',
    '#aec7e8', '#d62728', '#2ca02c', '#17becf'
]

# Create pie chart
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
wedges, texts, autotexts = ax.pie(
    counts,
    labels=segments,
    autopct='%.1f%%',
    startangle=90,
    colors=colors,
    textprops={'color': 'black', 'fontsize': 10}
)

# Add a white circle at the center to make it a donut
centre_circle = plt.Circle((0, 0), 0.70, fc='white')
fig.gca().add_artist(centre_circle)

# Title and layout
plt.title('Customer Segmentation Distribution', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Customer Segmentation Distribution (Donut Chart Analysis)¶

The donut chart provides a percentage breakdown of customers across RFM-based segments. Key insights:

  • Potential Loyalists (25.2%) form the largest share, showing strong potential for conversion into loyal customers with targeted engagement.
  • At Risk (20.7%) is the second largest group, signaling a significant churn risk. These customers require reactivation campaigns to prevent revenue loss.
  • Others (18.1%) represent a mixed category with moderate engagement. Further profiling can help design tailored strategies.
  • Loyal Customers (12.2%) consistently engage with the business. They should be nurtured with rewards and retention programs.
  • Lost (10.5%) are inactive customers. Win-back campaigns may be attempted, but prioritization depends on ROI.
  • Big Spenders (9.8%) contribute high monetary value despite lower frequency. Premium offers and personalized experiences can maximize their lifetime value.
  • Champions (3.5%) are the most valuable customers, combining high recency, frequency, and monetary scores. They should be prioritized for loyalty programs, advocacy, and exclusive benefits.

Strategic Takeaway:
The distribution highlights two critical priorities:

  1. Retention — Address the large At Risk segment to reduce churn.
  2. Growth — Convert Potential Loyalists into Loyal Customers to strengthen the core base.

Revenue Contribution by Segment Analysis¶

The bar chart highlights how different customer segments contribute to overall revenue. Key findings:

  • At Risk (₹5.36M) contributes the highest share of revenue, despite their declining engagement. This indicates that many high-value customers are at risk of churn, making retention efforts critical.
  • Potential Loyalists (₹5.09M) are the second-largest revenue drivers. With proper nurturing, they can be converted into Loyal Customers, strengthening the long-term revenue base.
  • Others (₹3.40M) and Loyal Customers (₹3.30M) contribute moderate revenue. Loyal Customers should be rewarded to maintain retention, while Others may need further profiling for targeted strategies.
  • Big Spenders (₹2.79M) generate significant revenue despite lower frequency. Personalized premium offers can maximize their lifetime value.
  • Lost (₹2.02M) still represent a notable revenue pool. Win-back campaigns may recover some value, though ROI should be carefully assessed.
  • Champions (₹1.10M), while the smallest group in count, remain strategically important due to their consistent high-value behavior. They should be prioritized for loyalty programs and advocacy initiatives.

Strategic Takeaway:
The analysis shows that the business is heavily dependent on At Risk and Potential Loyalist segments for revenue. Immediate focus should be on retaining At Risk customers and converting Potential Loyalists into Loyal Customers. Meanwhile, nurturing Champions and Big Spenders ensures sustained profitability and brand advocacy.

_Recency vs Monetary by Segment¶

# Scatter plot: Recency vs Monetary by Segment
plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
sns.scatterplot(data=df_rfm, x='Recency', y='Monetary', hue='Segment', palette='rainbow')
plt.title("Recency vs Monetary by Segment")
plt.xlabel("Recency (days since last purchase)")
plt.ylabel("Monetary (₹ total spend)")
plt.legend(title="Segment", bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Recency vs Monetary Analysis¶

This scatter plot compares Recency (days since last purchase) with Monetary (total spend), color-coded by segment:

  • Champions → Low recency (recent buyers), high monetary. Best customers.
  • Loyal Customers → Moderate recency, steady monetary. Reliable revenue.
  • Potential Loyalists → Low recency but lower spend. Opportunity to nurture.
  • At Risk → High recency (haven’t purchased recently) but high monetary. Critical to re-engage.
  • Big Spenders → High monetary, variable recency. Need VIP treatment.
  • Lost → High recency, low monetary. Minimal ROI.
  • Others → Mixed profiles, scattered across the plot.

Strategic Takeaway:
Customers with high spend but high recency (At Risk) are the most urgent to target, while Potential Loyalists represent the biggest growth opportunity.

8. Dashboard-Style KPI Cards¶

In [21]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# KPI metrics
total_revenue = df_rfm['Monetary'].sum()
total_customers = df_rfm.shape[0]
top_segment = df_rfm['Segment'].value_counts().idxmax()
at_risk_customers = df_rfm[df_rfm['Segment']=="At Risk"].shape[0]

# Display KPI cards
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(18,4))

# Card 1: Total Revenue
axes[0].barh(["Total Revenue"], [total_revenue], color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_title("₹ Revenue")

# Card 2: Total Customers
axes[1].barh(["Customers"], [total_customers], color="seagreen")
axes[1].set_title("Unique Customers")

# Card 3: Top Segment
axes[2].barh(["Top Segment"], [df_rfm['Segment'].value_counts().max()], color="orange")
axes[2].set_title(top_segment)

# Card 4: At Risk Customers
axes[3].barh(["At Risk"], [at_risk_customers], color="red")
axes[3].set_title("At Risk Customers")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

KPI Dashboard¶

The four KPI charts summarize the business performance and customer segmentation highlights:

  • ₹ Revenue (~20M)
    The company has generated strong overall revenue, reflecting healthy sales activity. This serves as the primary indicator of business scale and financial performance.

  • Unique Customers (~1,000)
    The customer base is sizable, providing a solid foundation for segmentation and targeted marketing. Maintaining engagement across this base is critical for sustained growth.

  • Potential Loyalists (~250 customers)
    This is the largest segment, representing customers with promising buying behavior. They are close to becoming Loyal Customers and should be nurtured with personalized offers and engagement strategies.

  • At Risk Customers (~200 customers)
    A significant portion of the customer base is at risk of churn. These customers contribute high revenue but show declining engagement, making retention campaigns essential to protect future earnings.

Strategic Takeaway:
The KPIs highlight a balanced picture: strong revenue and a healthy customer base, but with clear opportunities and risks. The business should focus on converting Potential Loyalists into Loyal Customers to strengthen retention, while simultaneously re‑engaging At Risk customers to prevent revenue leakage. Together, these actions will maximize customer lifetime value and ensure sustainable growth.
